question.prompt: Two fair dice, each with at least \(6\) faces are rolled. On each face of each die is printed a distinct integer from \(1\) to the number of faces on that die, inclusive. The probability of rolling a sum of \(7\) is \(\dfrac34\) of the probability of rolling a sum of \(10,\) and the probability of rolling a sum of \(12\) is \(\dfrac{1}{12}.\) What is the least possible number of faces on the two dice combined?

solutions.title: Prove a lower bound and attain it
solutions.explanation:
Both dice contain the numbers \(1\) through \(6\), so the number of outcomes summing to \(7\) is fixed. This turns the probability ratio into a counting condition.

Let the dice have \(a\le b\) faces. Their \(ab\) ordered outcomes are equally likely. Exactly six outcomes sum to \(7\):
\[
(1,6),(2,5),\ldots,(6,1).
\]
Since the two probabilities have the same denominator, the number of outcomes summing to \(10\) must be
\[
6\div\frac34=8.
\]

For each value on the smaller die, at most one value on the other die completes a sum of \(10\). Thus \(a\ge8\). Moreover, if both dice had at most eight faces, the only possible outcomes summing to \(10\) would be
\[
(2,8),(3,7),\ldots,(8,2),
\]
at most seven outcomes. Therefore \(b\ge9\), giving the universal lower bound
\[
a+b\ge8+9=17.
\]

Now take an \(8\)-faced die and a \(9\)-faced die. There are eight outcomes summing to \(10\), namely \((1,9)\) through \((8,2)\), so the required probability ratio is \(6/8=3/4\).

The outcomes summing to \(12\) are \((3,9),(4,8),\ldots,(8,4)\), exactly six. Hence
\[
\Pr(\text{sum }12)=\frac6{8\cdot9}=\frac1{12}.
\]
Both conditions hold, so the least combined number of faces is \(\boxed{17}\), choice \(\textbf{B}\).

solutions.title: Factor the sum-of-12 condition
solutions.explanation:
For small face counts, counting the outcomes summing to \(12\) produces an equation that factors. We will classify every possibility with at most \(17\) faces and check whether \(17\) is attainable.

Let \(6\le a\le b\) be the face counts, and suppose \(a+b\le17\). Then \(b\le11\), so both face counts are less than \(12\).

An outcome summing to \(12\) has the form \((x,12-x)\). It is allowed exactly when
\[
12-b\le x\le a.
\]
Every integer in this interval gives one distinct outcome, so there are
\[
a-(12-b)+1=a+b-11
\]
such outcomes. The given probability therefore implies
\[
\frac{a+b-11}{ab}=\frac1{12},
\qquad ab=12a+12b-132.
\]
Adding \(144\) after rearranging gives
\[
(12-a)(12-b)=12.
\]
The factors are positive integers, with \(12-a\ge12-b\) and \(12-a\le6\). Of the positive factor pairs \((12,1),(6,2),(4,3)\), only the last two satisfy these restrictions. Thus the only candidates are
\[
(a,b)=(6,10)\quad\text{or}\quad(8,9).
\]

Both have six outcomes summing to \(7\). Their counts for a sum of \(10\) are:

| Face counts | Outcomes summing to \(7\) | Outcomes summing to \(10\) |
|---|---:|---:|
| \((6,10)\) | 6 | 6 |
| \((8,9)\) | 6 | 8 |

For the last column, the first die can show any value from \(1\) through \(a\), and each has exactly one allowed partner completing a sum of \(10\). Thus only \((8,9)\) gives the required ratio \(6/8=3/4\). Its sum-of-12 probability is \(6/72=1/12\).

We have excluded every total below \(17\) and found a valid pair totaling \(17\). The minimum is therefore \(\boxed{17}\), choice \(\textbf{B}\).
